en: Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the Mahāvana-kūṭāgāra at Vaiśālī.

The Buddha was together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and eighty-four thousand great bodhisattvas; furthermore, surrounded by immeasurable multitudes of those in training and those beyond training, he preached the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Nāgavikramottararāja who rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has previously taught various sūtras containing the Buddha’s words, yet there are also those said not to be the Buddha’s words.
World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of this?
"How should it be received and upheld?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Nāgavikrāntagāmin-rāja, saying: "Good son!..."
Regarding what you have asked concerning that which is spoken as the word of the Buddha and that which is not the word of the Buddha within the various sūtras—O son of good family!
Such non-words are themselves the word of the Buddha.
"Good son! Reflect upon this well!
I shall now explain it to you thoroughly."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nāgavikramottara-rāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear [your teaching].”
The Buddha said,
"Good son, that which is called 'not speech' is itself the Buddha's speech."
"Good son! What is called the 'Buddha's word' is precisely what is termed the most weighty bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
All that I have taught is entirely without any bodily, verbal, or mental action that is not beneficial; yet therein there is no speech, no one who can speak, and no one who speaks."
"Good son! All that consists of form and speech is not the word of the Buddha.
If, O Dragon King, Supreme in Power and Virtue!"
That form is neither speech nor the Buddha’s speech; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are neither speech nor the Buddha’s speech.
Son of good family!
If there is no speech of form, and no speech of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is called the Buddha’s speech.
“Good son! If there are those who speak of bodily, verbal, or mental actions, it is not called the Buddha’s word; good son!
If there is speech that is devoid of the actions of body, mouth, and mind, this is called the Buddha’s speech. Good son!
If there is speech concerning earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth, it is not called the Buddha’s speech.
"Noble son! If there is that which does not speak of the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, this is called the Buddha's word. Noble son!"
If there are words of greed, hatred, or delusion, they are not called the Buddha’s words;
good son, if there are no words of greed, hatred, or delusion, these are called the Buddha’s words.
"Good son! If there is speech that is with outflows or speech that is without outflows, it is not called the Buddha’s speech; good son!"
That which is neither outflowing speech nor non-outflowing speech is called the Buddha’s speech. Good son!
If there is anything sought after, such speech is not called the Buddha’s speech, because that Buddha’s speech is free from seeking and longing.
"Good son! If there is neither high nor low, such speech as this is called the Buddha’s word. Good son!"
If there is speech that concerns a matter or speech that does not concern a matter, it is not called the Buddha’s word.
Good son! If there is speech that neither concerns a matter nor does not concern a matter, this is called the Buddha’s word.
"O son of good family!
If one says that there is a realization to be attained regarding the naturally pure dharma, that is not the word of the Buddha;
O son of good family!"
That which is neither of self-nature nor of other-nature is called the Buddha’s word. Good son!
That which contains both true speech and untrue speech is not called the Buddha’s word.
"Good son! If there is neither true speech nor untrue speech, this is called the Buddha’s word. Good son!"
If there were such [distinctions] as "these words are spoken by ordinary persons" or "these words are spoken by noble ones," they would not be called the Buddha's words; good son!
If there is neither the speech of ordinary people nor the speech of sages, this is called the Buddha’s speech. Good son!
If there is internal speech, external speech, or both internal and external speech, it is not called the Buddha’s speech.
"Good son! If there is no internal speech, no external speech, and no speech that is both internal and external, this is called the Buddha’s word. Good son!"

If, regarding all phenomena, there is speech that relies upon form as its basis, or relies upon feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as its basis, it is not called the Buddha’s word, O son of good family!

If, regarding all phenomena, there is no form upon which to rely, nor feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness upon which to rely—words spoken in this manner are called the Buddha’s words.
"Good son! If there are words spoken from any place that are the words of Māra or the words of the subjects of Māra, they are not called the words of the Buddha; good son!"
If there is no speech regarding any of the sense bases, that is called the Buddha’s word. Good son!

If one speaks based on the conceptual discrimination of the perception of form, or speaks based on the conceptual discrimination of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, it is not called the Buddha’s word.

“Good son! If one speaks without the conceptualization of the perception of form, and speaks without the conceptualization of the perceptions of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, this is called the Buddha’s word.”
For this reason, Māra and his followers shall find no opportunity.

Furthermore, noble son, one who is called a bodhisattva is so named because they regard form as selfless and do not discriminate it as "mine," and likewise regard feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as selfless and do not discriminate them as "mine. Such a person is called a bodhisattva.
Then the Bodhisattva Nāgavikramottararāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is there such verbal expression?”
“What is meant by ‘discourse’? The Buddha said, “Good son!

Mārapārṣadya... Furthermore, noble son, if a bodhisattva does not form the thought regarding form, "I shall be thus," and likewise does not form the thought regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, "I shall be thus," then such a bodhisattva has no speech whatsoever in any respect.
Nāgavikrāntagāmin-rāja!

Those noble sons who are most excellent have severed all speech, severed all obstructions, extinguished all conceit, cut through all nets, abandoned all dualistic views, and departed from all conceptualizations. Since they are without speech, how could there be any words?
Furthermore, there is nothing that can be spoken.
Therefore, that which is beyond speech is called the Buddha’s speech. Good son!
For this reason, you should know that this is the word of the Buddha:
"O son of good family!

If there is no body and no bodily action, no speech and no verbal action, no mind and no mental action; if it is neither action nor non-action, neither slander nor non-slander, neither produced nor arisen, without ideation and without location, without abiding and without passing away, neither quiescent nor active, a truthful speech that is immovable, yet not even immovable and thus not abiding, naturally without conditions and yet not without conditions—O son of good family!"
This is the Buddha’s word.
Because there is no possibility of speech therein, it is called the Buddha’s word.
"O son of good family!

When a bodhisattva has been able to train in this way, this is called training in the light of supreme wisdom, the Buddha’s words, the cooling words of the Buddha; it universally gladdens the bodies of all sentient beings and awakens the intentions of all sentient beings, leading them toward the Buddha-wisdom and causing them to uphold the meaning of the Dharma;

it universally gladdens the assembly of all bodhisattvas, awakening those who are asleep and enabling them to skillfully enter the Dharma-realm; it is the excellent determination that turns toward the Wheel of Dharma;

it turns the Wheel of Dharma, beats the great Dharma-drum, subdues the hosts of Māras, overcomes external enemies, and subdues all assemblies of non-Buddhists; it is able to rescue and protect those heading toward evil paths, it is able to adorn the worlds of all Buddhas, it is praised by all Buddhas, and such a one will certainly sit at the site of enlightenment.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva has already sat upon the seat of enlightenment; in this way, the Bodhisattva has already attained all the dhāraṇīs of a Bodhisattva.

When this Dharma-gate spoken by the Buddha was being taught, the Bodhisattva Noble Dragon Majestic Power King (Ārya-nāga-tejo-rāja) became fully perfected in the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) and immediately attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti);
twenty-six thousand Bodhisattvas likewise attained dhāraṇīs and various samādhis.
Eight thousand bhikṣus attained the dharma free from outflows.

Furthermore, eighty-four thousand sentient beings all resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and immediately, by means of their supernatural powers, rained down various flowers as an offering to the World-Honored One.

When the Tathāgata had spoken this Dharma-gate, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Noble Dragon Majestic Virtue King, along with the great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and all others present, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Sūtra on the Buddha’s Words
